title: The Fire With No End
hook: a column of fire no god could measure, and Ramana's first verse
carry: everything appears in one light: brahman
tomorrow: how much would you have to know to be called wise?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana's verses set aside the real-or-illusion fight: before judging the world, ask who is looking. Today, the hill where he wrote them, and the fire it's named for.

Two gods are arguing. Brahma, who makes the worlds, and Vishnu, who keeps them, each says: I'm the greatest. Then, between them, a column of fire splits the dark. No top in sight. No bottom. So they make a deal: whoever finds an end of it wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go on for ages. Neither finds an end. And then Brahma does something you don't expect from the god of creation.
screen: `TWO GODS, ONE COLUMN OF FIRE.` → `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` → `NEITHER FINDS AN END.`

segments.voice: He lies. He comes back and says he saw the top. Vishnu admits he never found the bottom. Then the fire opens, and Shiva steps out of it: the column was Shiva all along, the light nobody can get outside of to measure. For the lie, Shiva says Brahma won't be worshipped the way the others are, which is how many families explain why so few temples are his. That's the Shiva Purana, and in Tamil Nadu the story has an address. Arunachala, the hill at Tiruvannamalai, is honored as that fire become a hill. Every year, in the month of Karthigai, a huge flame is lit on its summit, and the crowds below bow to it. A boy of sixteen named Ramana came to that hill in 1896 and never left. Decades later he wrote his Forty Verses, and its first verse names that same one light. In paraphrase: since we see a world, we accept one source with many powers; the picture of names and forms, the one who watches it, the screen and the light, all of these are that one. Here's the teaching, plainly. Hindus call that one source Brahman: not one more thing in the picture, but what every picture shows up in. A few verses on, Ramana adds that world and mind rise and set together. What they rise in, the light that stays, is what is. Brahma tried to stand outside the light and measure it. Nobody can. Everyone's already in it.
screen: `THE FIRE OPENS: SHIVA.` · `ARUNACHALA: THE FIRE AS A HILL.` · `KARTHIGAI: A FLAME ON THE SUMMIT.` · `PICTURE, WATCHER, SCREEN, LIGHT: ONE.` · then, large: `BRAHMAN: WHAT EVERY PICTURE IS IN.`

segments.voice: If you have a lamp or a candle and it's safe to light, light it and rest your eyes on the flame for the sit. If not, picture the Karthigai flame on the dark hill. Thoughts and sounds will come and go. Let them rise and set in the light, the way every scene plays on one screen.
Ramana's Forty Verses: a Tamil poem, written at the foot of the fire-hill, that opens by calling every picture, watcher and light one.
The line to take with you: everything appears in one light, Brahman. A god flew for ages and never found its edge.

howItsDone: At Tiruvannamalai the Karthigai Deepam flame is lit on Arunachala's summit each year, and many Tamil Hindu families light rows of lamps at home that night; Ramana's followers sit with his first verse as an entry into the poem.

Arunachala.meaning: the holy hill at Tiruvannamalai, honored as Shiva's fire

Brahman.meaning: the one reality every picture appears in

nama-rupa.meaning: names and forms: what every picture is made of

Ramana.meaning: Ramana Maharshi, a sage who lived at Arunachala
